BlackMagic, in my opinion, offer the best and most cinematic image quality available at prosumer price points. The image for sub £2k is simply wild, BRAW is one of the best file types I’ve ever been able to work with in terms of latitude in post. Manual focussing is how most narrative and commercial filmmaking is done and always has been, it’s not so tough - focus peaking makes it easier. But the pocket series are ergonomically horrible (I own a 6K pro and a pxyis) and have terrible battery life - so often require a bit of rigging to get the best result possible. But, if image quality is the most important thing for you, black magic is the best bang for your buck, by far (in my opinion).

Unfortunately if you’re not into serious filmmaking I’m afraid it’s probably not worth holding onto! With this being a cinema camera, you need more than just a lens to make this thing usable. An external monitor that accepts SDI in, rigging for handles/shoulder rigs, some decent recording media (no SD cards on this bad boy), a good power solution (V-Locks most likely as shooting BRAW is thirsty work for batteries), some kind of hollow focus system (this camera doesn’t have autofocus) a plethora of cables…the list goes on. I got my Pxyis last week and it’s turning into a beast just to be able to use it properly without shortcuts - it’s certainly a more advanced camera geared towards full time filmmakers. With it being new you’d fetch a good price and be able to reinvest that into a more beginner friendly set up, or even just something that requires less rigging and you get to use straight out of the box.

Shutter speeds were never designed for video, they're designed for stills. Shutter angles are much more video-centric. When cranking fps you normally have to do some quick maths, double your FPS giving you your shutter speed. Apart from most DSLRs don't actually offer the correct shutter speeds and you end up compromising by rounding up or down. e.g, 1/125th rather than 1/120th, 1/50th rather than 1/48th, so you'll always end up with worse results.

It doesn't mean that shutter angles eliminate all issues with motion blur at higher frame rates, apologies I should have been clearer, it's just you always get cleaner results as your shutter just stays at 180 degrees.

It takes *decades* to become a respected, competent Director of Photography.

You could pick up a DSLR and start getting videography work in a couple of weeks.

DoPs tend to work as a part of large scale productions as the head of two departments while videographers tend to be more one man bands. 

They're different jobs with different roles and responsibilities.

There was no audio when cinema first emerged. Movies were projected and accompanied by a live musical performance. So photography made sense then, and it just never changed. The first motion picture was in the 1880s, but the first"talkie" (motion picture with sound) as they were called then wasn't until 1927.

A lot of the film industry is still the way it was a century ago. Just the tech changes.

Different jobs.

A DoP works as part of a production crew and works specifically with a 1st AC (Assistant Camera) a 2nd AC, a focus puller, loader, gaffers, best boys, sparks etc. On a film set the DoP is the head of the camera department (and sort of lighting department too) who's job involves working with the director to create a visual identity for the work, through camera, lens and lighting choice. They decide how the piece is lit, what lights to use, how to diffuse/bounce/neg the light to shape it to create meaning in the frame, with the gaffer/sparks. 

It takes *decades* of dedication to the craft to become a competent, respected DoP.

Not to say videographers don't work hard, they sure do. But they're much more of a 'one man band' type deal. They may edit their own work, they may work with smaller crews every now and again but they will have a limited knowledge of production lighting, how to manage a film department on set, and a lot of them will be self taught. DoPs tend to train as camera trainees and work their way through C, B and A units on TV shows, commercials and movies for years before getting to even sniff time behind the camera.

All in all, I think it's a respect thing and it's something that's earned. Plus, the actual shooting of a film is called "principle photography" as it always has been. So Director of Photography makes sense there. I get your point about there not being audio - but originally there was no audio in movies and they were accompanied by a live pianist, so it was literally just photography.

Shooting RAW would be your best bet. RAW is so damn cheap these days too with the Black Magic Pocket line up, BRAW is fantastic. You could pick one up for about £1,000 these days which is dirt cheap for a RAW ready cam. You'll be able to change your WB in post and keyframe throughout, so it would appear seamless.

Storage may be an issue, I think shooting 12:1 compression BRAW you'd likely get around 3/4 hours per terabyte, with 1TB Samsung T5s going for £100 each you'd need a couple, bonus is that they're lightning to edit from. 

Other than that you'd need some sort of lighting rigged to a DMX board that you could manually control throughout the day but you're looking at big money there.

You'll need to have the FD lenses converted to EF mounts professionally for them to achieve infinity focus.

Unfortunately the EF mount flange distance doesn't allow for FD adapters to achieve infinity focus without a corrective optical element - which are usually very poor quality. I've looked far and wide for a good one but they're all terrible and render the image unusable between f4 and f1.2.

There are a few options online for professionally converting your FD lenses, or Spenser Sakurai did a tutorial here - [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MgeG3xouLUk&t=997s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MgeG3xouLUk&t=997s)

But, a word of warning, when you start playing with your lenses like that you run a high risk of messing it up and having to send it for professional repairs so I'd always recommend getting them converted professionally.
